# `protocol_step_order`: a role body takes a step its protocol does not allow yet

An `@[endpoints]` protocol generates one state per step of each role, and a
role body moves from state to state by calling the generated functions:
`send_…`, `recv_…`, `choose_…`, `offer_…`, `close`. Each function takes the
state it is the next step from. Calling one with a state the role is not in
yet, or no longer in, is this error. It says what the call tries to do, what
the protocol says the role must do at that point, and points at that step of
the protocol. It also draws the conversation so far: the protocol's steps up to
that point, the role's own marked `done`, the one it must take next, and the
one it tried (inside a `loop`, drawn as one round; inside a `choose`, as the
branch taken).

## A program that triggers it

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO
  needs Session.Live
  @[endpoints]
  protocol Stream do
    loop do
      Prod -> Cons : Int
      choose by Cons:
        more -> Cons -> Prod : Bool
        done -> Cons -> Prod : Bool
                stop
      end
    end
  end
  pfn cons(s : Cap(Session.Live), st : Stream_Cons.S_recv_Msg_Prod_Cons_1) : Stream_Cons.Yield do
    Stream_Cons.close(s, Stream_Cons.choose_done(s, st, true))
  end
  fn main(c : Cap(IO)) do () end
end
```

`Cons` chooses `done` before it has received the `Int` that `Prod` sends at the
top of each round.

## The fix

Take the step the error names first, then go on from the state it gives you:

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO
  needs Session.Live
  @[endpoints]
  protocol Stream do
    loop do
      Prod -> Cons : Int
      choose by Cons:
        more -> Cons -> Prod : Bool
        done -> Cons -> Prod : Bool
                stop
      end
    end
  end
  pfn cons(s : Cap(Session.Live), st : Stream_Cons.S_recv_Msg_Prod_Cons_1) : Stream_Cons.Yield do
    Stream_Cons.recv_Msg_Prod_Cons_1(s, st, fn (_n, st1) ->
      Stream_Cons.close(s, Stream_Cons.choose_done(s, st1, true)))
  end
  fn main(c : Cap(IO)) do () end
end
```

Inside a `loop`, the step after the last one of a round is the first one of
the next: after `more`, a role is back at the top of the loop, so it cannot
`close` there.

## Why the rule exists

The protocol is the contract every role is checked against. A body that takes
its steps in another order would send a message its peer is not waiting for,
or wait for one that never comes, and both deadlock the session at run time.
Typing each state separately turns that into a compile-time error at the call
that goes out of order.

See also: [writing each role](../choreography.md#step-3-write-each-role).
